484.title: Devarim: how can I alone? (Deuteronomy 1:12)
484.hook: Moses' "how" is chanted to the tune of Lamentations before Tisha B'Av
484.howItsDone: On the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, many congregations chant Deuteronomy 1:12, which begins with eicha, in the mournful melody used for the book of Lamentations on Tisha B'Av itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devarim and the judges' charge: a penny case as precious as a fortune. Your line was small and great alike. Today, one word changes the music in the synagogue.

It's the Sabbath just before Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the destruction of the Temples in Jerusalem. The reader at the Torah is chanting Devarim in the usual melody, the one the congregation has heard all year. Then, on one verse, the tune turns. It drops into a slow, sad melody that everyone in the room recognizes. It's the melody of the book of Lamentations, which they'll hear on the floor in the dim light a few days later. All on account of a single word.
screen: `THE SABBATH BEFORE TISHA B'AV.` → `THE TUNE TURNS ON ONE VERSE.` → `THE MELODY OF LAMENTATIONS.`

segments.voice: The verse is Moses, remembering how worn out he was in the wilderness. In the old Jewish translation: "How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife?" The first word in Hebrew is eicha. How. Not a calm how, like how do I fix this. A cry. And it's the same word that opens the book of Lamentations: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!" That book is even called Eicha in Hebrew. The midrash on Lamentations noticed that three prophets used this word: Moses here, Isaiah looking at a faithful city gone wrong, and Jeremiah over the ruins of Jerusalem. Moses saw the people at ease, the midrash says, Isaiah saw them restless, and Jeremiah saw them broken. So the reader borrows Lamentations' melody for Moses' verse, and the whole room hears where the road can lead. But look at what Moses does with his eicha. He doesn't just sigh. He divides the load. He tells the people to bring wise, understanding men from each tribe, and he makes them heads over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens. The path met this weariness twice already this year, with Jethro's advice and with the seventy elders. Deuteronomy tells it from Moses' own side, years later, and lets one word carry the feeling. In this story, saying how can I alone isn't a failure. It's the sentence that comes right before help.

segments.voice: Let your mind go to whatever has been too heavy lately: a sick parent, a project, a child who's struggling. Don't solve it; just say quietly, the way Moses did, how can I alone, and let it be a sigh, not a plan. Then let one name come to mind, someone you could say it to.
Eicha. How, as a cry. Moses' word in Deuteronomy, and the first word and Hebrew name of the book of Lamentations.
Your line: how can I alone. Even Moses needed others to share the load. See you tomorrow.

485.title: Devarim: the scouts retold (Deuteronomy 1:22–46)
485.hook: Moses retells an old failure so it won't be repeated
485.carry: tell it so it won't repeat
485.howItsDone: The portion Devarim, with Moses' retelling of the scouts, is read on the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, and the Mishnah counts the decree on the wilderness generation among the calamities remembered on that fast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, eicha: Moses' cry, how can I alone, chanted in the tune of Lamentations. Your line was how can I alone. Today, the journey's oldest failure, told again.

After a team fails at something big, there's a choice. Bury it, and hope nobody brings it up. Or walk through it step by step: what was decided, what everyone told themselves, where it went wrong. It's the meeting nobody puts on the calendar gladly. Moses, standing at the Jordan with a new generation, holds it. He takes the worst moment of the forty years, the twelve scouts and the night the people wept, and tells it again, in detail, to the children of the people who lived it.
screen: `BURY IT, OR WALK THROUGH IT.` → `THE MEETING NOBODY WANTS.` → `MOSES HOLDS IT.`

segments.voice: The path read this story back in Numbers. Twelve scouts go in, ten come back terrified, the people weep all night, and that generation is told it will die in the wilderness. Now listen to Moses' version, and notice what he changes. In his telling, the idea of scouts starts with the people. You all came to me, he says, and asked to send men ahead to search out the land. And he admits, the idea pleased me. He doesn't hide behind God's command. He puts his own yes in the story. Then he tells it plainly. The land was good, even the scouts said so, but the people murmured in their tents and said God must hate us. And then the part that's easy to forget: after the decree, a group tried to fix it by force. They marched up into the hill country without God's blessing, and the Amorites chased them, Moses says, the way bees chase. Panic, and then overcorrection. Two mistakes, not one. The rabbis tied that night of weeping to a date. The Mishnah lists it first among the disasters of the ninth of Av, and the Talmud imagines God saying: you wept for nothing that night, so it will become a night of weeping for generations. And Devarim is read on the Sabbath right before Tisha B'Av. Moses tells it so it won't be repeated. Honest about his part, honest about both mistakes.

Devarim. Words, and the book where Moses retells even the failures, so the next generation doesn't live them twice.

486.title: Devarim: pass by gently (Deuteronomy 2:4–9)
486.hook: Israel must pass Edom and Moab without taking their land
486.howItsDone: This passage is read in synagogues as part of Devarim, the first portion of Deuteronomy, and some commentators point to it as an example of the Torah recognizing the land rights of Israel's neighbors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devarim and the scouts retold, Moses' own part included. Your line was tell it so it won't repeat. Today, a march past other people's land.

A huge crowd on the move, tired of the desert, and suddenly strong. Ahead of them is a mountain country with food and water to sell, and the people who live there are, the text says, afraid of them. In plenty of old war stories, the big crowd takes what it wants. Moses remembers the order that came instead. Walk past. Pay for your water. Don't take a single footstep of their land. It's a quiet moment in his farewell, and a strange order to give an army.
screen: `A STRONG CROWD, A MOUNTAIN COUNTRY.` → `THEY ARE AFRAID OF YOU.` → `WALK PAST.`

segments.voice: The first neighbors are the children of Esau in Seir, the people of Edom. Moses calls them your brothers, because Esau was Jacob's twin. God's instruction, as Moses retells it: they'll be afraid of you, so take good care of yourselves, and don't start a fight. I won't give you any of their land, not even enough to set the sole of your foot on, because I gave Mount Seir to Esau. Buy food from them with money, and buy water to drink. And then a line that sounds almost like a parent: "these forty years the LORD thy God hath been with thee; thou hast lacked nothing." In other words, you don't need what's theirs. You never did. Then Moab, the descendants of Lot, Abraham's nephew. Same rule. Don't harass them, don't go to war, their land was given to them too. Notice what that means. In this telling, the God who promised Israel a land also gave other peoples their lands, and expects Israel to honor the boundary even when it could be crossed easily. Numbers remembers that Edom actually refused Israel passage, and Israel went around. Deuteronomy doesn't dwell on the insult. It remembers the rule: their land isn't yours, and fear doesn't make it yours. In this telling, a strong people's power shows partly in what it walks past.

segments.voice: Think of a place where you have a little power: a younger sibling, a new hire, a conversation you could easily take over. Let the line sit with you, thou hast lacked nothing, and notice what you already have. Then picture walking past what isn't yours, without resentment.
Devarim. Words, and in them a march where the strong side pays for its water and walks around.
Your line: pass by gently. Like the people passing Edom, you have lacked nothing. Until tomorrow.

487.title: Va'etchanan: and I pleaded (Deuteronomy 3:23–26)
487.hook: Moses begs to enter the land and hears "Let it suffice thee"
487.tomorrow: Va'etchanan: don't forget what you saw (Deuteronomy 4:9)
487.howItsDone: Va'etchanan is read in synagogues on the Sabbath after Tisha B'Av, known as Shabbat Nachamu, the Sabbath of comfort, named for the prophetic reading from Isaiah that follows it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devarim's march past Edom and Moab, paying for water. Your line was pass by gently. Today a new portion opens, and Moses asks for something he won't get.

Forty years of work. Every crisis carried. And now, with the far bank of the river in sight, the word comes: you won't cross it. Someone else will. Moses knew this already; it was decided back at the rock in Numbers. But in his farewell he tells his people something they may not have known: that he went back and asked. He begged. The new portion takes its name from that begging.
screen: `FORTY YEARS, AND THE FAR BANK IN SIGHT.` → `SOMEONE ELSE WILL CROSS.` → `HE WENT BACK AND ASKED.`

segments.voice: It begins, in the old Jewish translation: "And I besought the LORD at that time, saying." The Hebrew first word is va'etchanan, and I pleaded, from the root for grace or favor. Rashi hears in it a request for a free gift, something not earned. And what he asks is simple: "Let me go over, I pray Thee, and see the good land." Just let me see it. The rabbis noticed how hard he asked. A midrash counts the letters of va'etchanan as numbers, and they add up to five hundred fifteen, so the midrash says Moses prayed five hundred fifteen prayers to enter. Then the answer: "Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto Me of this matter." In Hebrew, rav lach. Literally, much to you, or enough for you. It's a no. A final one. But it isn't silent, and it isn't the end of the conversation. In the next breath God tells him to climb to the top of Pisgah and look west, north, south and east, and see the land with his eyes. And to strengthen Joshua, who will lead them across. Rashi hears more than a refusal in rav lach: much good, he says, is already stored up for you. The portion is read on the Sabbath right after Tisha B'Av, called the Sabbath of comfort. The comfort starts with a man who heard no, and still climbed the mountain to look.

segments.voice: Think of a no you've been given lately: a job, an answer, a body that won't do what it used to. Feel how much you wanted it, then say softly, rav lach, enough for you. Look around the way Moses looked out from the mountain, and name three things you can see from where you stand.
Va'etchanan. And I pleaded. Moses' first word in this portion, asking for grace he knows he can't demand.
Your line: let it suffice thee. A no can still come with a view. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

488.title: Va'etchanan: don't forget what you saw (Deuteronomy 4:9)
488.hook: take heed lest you forget, and make it known to your children
488.howItsDone: Some Jewish prayer books include a short list of things to remember daily, and the day of Sinai, drawn from Deuteronomy 4:9–10, is one of them; Nachmanides counts not forgetting Sinai as a commandment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Va'etchanan: Moses pleaded, and heard rav lach. Your line was let it suffice thee. Today, a warning about memory.

Ask someone who lived through a big day where they were, and you may hear the room, the radio, the weather. Ask their grandchildren about the same day, and you may get a sentence from a textbook. Memory thins as it travels. A few generations, and a day that changed a family can become a date nobody can quite place. Moses is speaking to people who were children at Sinai, or not yet born, and he seems to know how this goes. So he stops in the middle of his speech and gives them a warning.
screen: `THE ROOM, THE RADIO, THE WEATHER.` → `A LINE FROM A TEXTBOOK.` → `MOSES STOPS TO WARN THEM.`

segments.voice: The warning, in the old Jewish translation, begins: "Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget." Forget what? The things your eyes saw. He means Sinai: the day you stood before God at Horeb, the mountain burning, the voice out of the fire. And the verse goes on: don't let them slip from your heart all the days of your life, but make them known to your children and your children's children. Notice the order. First, guard yourself. Take heed. In Hebrew, hishamer lecha, watch yourself, be on guard. Memory isn't automatic; it's something you protect, like a flame in wind. Then, pass it on. Not as a lecture. As testimony: what your eyes saw. The medieval teacher Nachmanides, called the Ramban, read this verse as a full commandment, to never let the experience of Sinai leave your mind, and to tell it to every generation. And there's a curious afterlife to the words keep thy soul diligently. Later teachers heard in them a duty to look after your own body and life too, so the verse about memory became a verse about health. Both readings meet in the same place. What you were given has to be guarded, or it's gone. Moses can't make his listeners' grandchildren remember Sinai. He can only make sure his listeners don't forget, and tell it.

segments.voice: Let one moment come back that you never want to lose: a birth, a goodbye, a kindness, a moment that felt holy or just true. Don't explain it; see it, where you stood, what you heard, who was there. Hold it until you could tell it the way your eyes saw it, so someone younger could hear it one day.
Va'etchanan. And I pleaded. The portion where Moses, after his own no, turns to guarding what his people saw.
Your line: don't forget what you saw. Memory is something you guard. See you tomorrow.

489.title: Va'etchanan: the Shema whole (Deuteronomy 6:4–9)
489.hook: love God with all your heart, soul and might
489.tomorrow: Va'etchanan: at home and on the way (Deuteronomy 6:7)
489.howItsDone: Jews recite the Shema and the V'ahavta paragraph in the morning and evening services and at bedtime, many covering their eyes for the first line; the passage is also written inside the mezuzah and tefillin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Va'etchanan's warning: guard what you saw, and tell it. Your line was don't forget what you saw. Today, the words Jews say morning and night, in their home chapter.

Many Jewish children learn the Shema before they can read: six Hebrew words, said with a hand over the eyes. It's said at bedtime, in the morning service and the evening service, and for many centuries it has been the words Jews hoped to say at the very end of life. The first line is often said on its own, like a motto. In the Torah it isn't on its own at all. It sits in Moses' farewell, in the sixth chapter of Deuteronomy, and the very next word opens a paragraph.
screen: `SIX WORDS, A HAND OVER THE EYES.` → `MORNING, NIGHT, AND THE END.` → `THE WORD THAT FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: First the line, in the old Jewish translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Then, without a pause in the text: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." The first Hebrew word of that second verse is today's word. V'ahavta. And thou shalt love. It names the whole paragraph that Jews say right after the Shema. And it raises a question the rabbis took seriously: can love be commanded? The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, answers by taking the three phrases one at a time. With all thy heart: the Hebrew spells heart here with a doubled letter, levavcha, and the Mishnah hears two hearts, so love God with both your inclinations, the good one and the selfish one. Your whole messy self, not just your best moods. With all thy soul: even if your life is taken. The Talmud tells that Rabbi Akiva, dying under Roman torture, said the Shema and drew out the final word, one, until his breath ended. With all thy might: the Mishnah reads it as with all your money, your resources. And it adds one more: for whatever measure is measured out to you, good or bad, give thanks. So the command isn't to feel warm. It's to bring everything, the good impulses and the bad, your life, your wallet, your luck, into one direction. The paragraph that follows tells how: these words on your heart, taught to your children, on your doorposts. That's tomorrow.
screen: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `V'AHAVTA: AND THOU SHALT LOVE.` · `BOTH HEARTS, YOUR LIFE, YOUR MIGHT.` · `EVERY MEASURE, GOOD OR BAD.` · then, large: `WITH ALL YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: If you pray, cover your eyes and say the first line, Shema Yisrael, in Hebrew or English, then the next verse slowly, a breath between each phrase. If you don't, hold the three phrases as questions: what would all your heart include, what do you give your life to, and where does your might, your money and your time, actually go?
V'ahavta. And thou shalt love. The verse after the Shema, and the name of the paragraph said with it, morning and night.
Your line: with all your heart. The messy parts count too. That's day four hundred eighty-nine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, v'ahavta: love with both hearts, with your life and your might. Your line was with all your heart. Today, where those words are meant to live.

The real conversations in a family often happen sideways. Not always at the formal dinner. Sometimes in the car, eyes on the road, when nobody has to look at anybody. Or at the edge of a bed, lights off, when a kid suddenly asks the big question. Or in the kitchen at seven in the morning, half awake. The paragraph after the Shema seems to know this. It doesn't schedule a weekly lesson. It names four ordinary places where words can be spoken, and an ordinary day already passes through them.
screen: `IN THE CAR, EYES ON THE ROAD.` → `THE EDGE OF THE BED.` → `FOUR ORDINARY PLACES.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the old Jewish translation: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Teach them diligently is one Hebrew word, v'shinantam, and early readers hear sharpen in it, while others hear repeat. Say it until it's sharp. And talk of them, v'dibarta bam: not preach, talk. Then the four places. Sitting at home, walking on the road, lying down, rising up. The rabbis read the last pair as times. That's why the Shema is said at night and in the morning. But they argued about the posture. The Mishnah records it. The school of Shammai said: at night, recline, and in the morning, stand, because the verse says lying down and rising up. The school of Hillel said: everyone says it in their own way, however they happen to be, because the verse also says when thou walkest by the way. Read that way, the verse isn't asking you to arrange your body for the words. It's asking the words to come along wherever your body already is. The Mishnah even tells of Rabbi Tarfon, who lay down by the road at night to follow Shammai's ruling and put himself in danger from robbers. His colleagues told him he deserved what nearly happened, for setting aside Hillel's view.
screen: `V'SHINANTAM: SHARPEN, REPEAT.` · `TALK, DON'T PREACH.` · `LYING DOWN AND RISING: NIGHT AND MORNING.` · `HILLEL: AS YOU ARE, ON THE WAY.` · then, large: `AT HOME AND ON THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Think of the four places in your own day: home, the road, bedtime, the morning. Pick the one that has another person in it, and one thing that matters to you that you haven't said in a while: a hope, a worry, a story. Let it become a sentence or two you could say right where you already are.
Va'etchanan. And I pleaded. The portion that holds the Shema, and the four places its words are meant to travel.
Your line: at home and on the way. The week held eicha, the scouts, the gentle march, a pleading, a memory, the Shema, and now its places. Day four hundred ninety, in the books.
